en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Bhūtagāmavagga 15.
The Second Training Rule on Lodgings.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, there were seventeen groups of monks who were companions.
While staying, they stayed together; when departing, they departed together.

Having spread out bedding in a certain monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, when they departed, they neither removed it themselves nor had it removed by others, and they departed without having asked for permission.
The lodgings were infested with termites.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can the group-of-seventeen monks, having spread out bedding in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, depart without putting it away?"
“They will neither lift it up themselves nor have it lifted up; they will depart without asking permission, leaving the lodging infested with termites.
Then those monks, having rebuked the group of seventeen monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One said:
“Is it true, monks, that the group of seventeen monks, having spread out bedding in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha…”
“Did those departing neither take it up themselves nor have it taken up, but departed without asking permission, leaving the lodgings eaten by termites?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him... [as before]...

"How indeed, monks, can those foolish men, having spread out bedding in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, depart without either putting it away themselves or having it put away by others, and depart without informing anyone, so that the lodgings are eaten by termites?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on]."
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:

“Whosoever, however, a monk, having spread out a bed in a dwelling belonging to the Sangha, or having had it spread out, when departing does not either remove it himself or have it removed, or departs without asking permission, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Whosoever, however:
Whoever is such a person … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … [and so on] … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
A "monastery belonging to the Sangha" (saṅghika) is one that has been given to the Sangha and relinquished as their property.
A "bed" (seyyā), namely—
A mattress, a bolster, an upper blanket, a ground-covering, a wooden board, a piece of hide, a sitting mat, a bedspread, a grass mat, or a leaf mat.
"Having spread out" means having spread it out oneself.
"Having had it spread out" means having had another [mat] spread out.
"While departing, he does not remove it" means:
One should not pull it out oneself.
"One should not have it pulled out" means one should not have another person pull it out.
"Or he may go without asking permission":

if a monk goes beyond the enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or beyond the precincts of an unenclosed monastery, without having asked permission from a monk, a novice, or a monastery attendant, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If he goes beyond the precincts of an unenclosed monastery, there is an offense of expiation.

If, regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha, one perceives it as belonging to the Saṅgha, and having spread out a bed or having had it spread out, one departs without either putting it away oneself or having it put away, or goes without asking permission, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If, regarding what belongs to the Saṅgha, one is doubtful, and having spread out a bed or having had it spread out, one departs without either putting it away oneself or having it put away, or goes without asking permission, there is an offense of expiation.

If one spreads out a bed belonging to the Saṅgha, perceiving it as belonging to an individual, and having spread it out or caused it to be spread out, departs without either putting it away or causing it to be put away, or departs without asking permission, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If one spreads out a bed in the vicinity of a monastery, in a hall for attendance, in a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree, and having spread it out or caused it to be spread out, departs without either putting it away or causing it to be put away, or departs without asking permission... [there is an offense of expiation].
If he should go [without doing so], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Having spread out, or having had spread out, a bed or a bench in a dwelling, or in the vicinity of a dwelling, or in a meeting hall, or in a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree,
if he departs without either picking it up himself or having it picked up, [there is an offense].
Or if one should go without asking permission, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is [actually] private property but one perceives it as belonging to the Saṅgha, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one is doubtful regarding private property, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it belongs to another individual and he perceives it as belonging to another individual, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it belongs to himself, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
He goes after having lifted [the goods] himself; he goes after having had them lifted by another;
he goes after having asked for permission.
It is obstructed by something;
having gone while still having expectations, he stands there and asks for permission;
it is obstructed by something.
In times of distress,
for one who is insane,
and for the first offender.
The fifth training rule on lodgings is finished.
